episode_thesis: Mark (captioned 'Mark rinsky') argues that systematic trend following should be run and judged as a full system (signals, diversified portfolio construction, risk management), where market selection, realistic backtests and humility about models matter more than clever new techniques, and that when valuation and macro arguments cut both ways one should follow price trends. He adds a macro thread (heavy Treasury bill issuance acting as de facto QE that offsets Fed tightening) and cites the GIC/JPMorgan hedge-fund framework as an unintended case for trend following as loss mitigation. The host reports a three-month giveback for trend followers in July 2024 and agrees that drawdowns are entry points, that markets should not be dropped for past losses (cocoa) and that volatility floors guard against suppressed volatility.

speakers.name: Mark rinsky (caption spelling; Systematic Investor co-host)
speakers.role: Rules-based investor / trend-following practitioner and manager evaluator, co-host of the Systematic Investor series
speakers.speaker_note: Name is as captioned in the transcript and ledger. Listener questions (Philip) are read by Niels and are not Mark's views. The ledger's speaker label is used for Mark throughout; no speaker confusion found between the two voices.

worldview_premises.premise: Heavy Treasury bill issuance relative to coupons acts as de facto quantitative easing: bills are near-money and usable as collateral, fewer coupons make risky long-duration supply scarcer and lower long-term rates, offsetting the Fed's tightening.
worldview_premises.support: Cites a Hudson Bay Capital paper on activist Treasury issuance and describes the size of the issuance difference as 'staggering'; no figures given on air.

worldview_premises.premise: The 2016 money market fund rules raised structural demand for short-term instruments, giving Treasury room to issue more bills; Treasury's rule of thumb is about 15% bills, but actual issuance has been much higher.
worldview_premises.support: Regulatory history and Treasury practice recalled from memory.

worldview_premises.premise: Net duration supply (Fed QT runoff plus coupon issuance) is what matters; Fed balance-sheet runoff adds coupon supply each month and a Treasury cut in coupon issuance offsets it.
worldview_premises.support: Supply-and-demand reasoning along the yield curve.

worldview_premises.premise: The cost of crisis alpha and low correlation is poor performance in calm, sideways markets with lower rate and inflation volatility, and investors forget the crisis benefit when they rebalance on recent results.
worldview_premises.support: Practitioner experience with investor behaviour.

worldview_premises.premise: Past losses are not a reason to drop a market: it may be a diversifier whose future is unknown, and one-sided-market assumptions fail (short-term interest rates went below zero after he had judged them one-sided).
worldview_premises.support: Personal anecdotes: an argument with a large trend follower about a five-year losing market; his own wrong forecast on the zero bound.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets with central-bank intervention (managed FX) that punish speculators justify lower exposure; the best markets are two-sided with hedgers and speculators, with retail participation, because markets of only professional traders are harder to make money in.
worldview_premises.support: Market-review criteria used at his earlier firm; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Illiquidity brings jump risk, so a market falling below minimum volume or open interest should be dropped, and brand-new markets avoided; screening should go into adding markets carefully because removal is hard to decide well.
worldview_premises.support: Market-review practice.

worldview_premises.premise: A market review should look at how a market earned or lost money (one trade or many, choppiness), not just whether it made money.
worldview_premises.support: Practice description.

worldview_premises.premise: Commodity markets whose prices governments can manage (like cocoa) look like poor trend markets, yet can still produce explosive trends after a supply dislocation; an index excluding cocoa (Credit Suisse managed futures) underperformed CTAs that held it; few markets are dropped except for liquidity.
worldview_premises.support: Index comparison from memory; no figures.

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility targeting raises size when volatility is artificially low (Swiss franc peg), which was the worst action when the peg broke.
worldview_premises.support: Swiss franc peg episode.

worldview_premises.premise: Backtests are valuable not for performance or Sharpe ('I've never seen a bad backtest') but for what they reveal about the manager's care in research, assumptions and treatment of transaction costs; investors' Sharpe thresholds conflict, so the research process matters more than the numbers.
worldview_premises.support: His paper 'I've never seen a bad backtest'; anecdote of two Manhattan investors with opposite Sharpe thresholds (reject below 2 versus reject above 1.25).

worldview_premises.premise: Anyone can build a good model; what matters is applying it across many markets, building portfolios and a full system, and moving from the backtest (laboratory) to a factory with realistic inputs, outputs, timing, costs and execution.
worldview_premises.support: Scientist versus engineer analogy.

worldview_premises.premise: A systematic manager should be evaluated on return generation, portfolio construction and risk management; regression or model-based signals risk parameter instability so simple rules are preferred; diversification is the one free lunch.
worldview_premises.support: Manager evaluation experience; Markowitz-style free lunch idea.

worldview_premises.premise: Risk management belongs inside the model's entry and exit rules, with a stop loss as a fail-safe protecting investor principal.
worldview_premises.support: Mike Tyson 'punched in the nose' quote.

worldview_premises.premise: When stock-bond correlation turns positive, 60/40 volatility rises and bonds lose their diversification role, so risk must be monitored via the off-diagonal correlation terms and the stock-versus-bond choice becomes one of relative valuation.
worldview_premises.support: Covariance-matrix reasoning.

worldview_premises.premise: In the GIC/JPMorgan framework trend following meets all three criteria (low equity correlation, drawdown mitigation, positive alpha after beta); managed futures ranked second for alpha after beta behind global macro; trend following is not an equity substitute.
worldview_premises.support: His reading of the GIC/JPM paper; he stresses the paper was not written as a case for trend following.

worldview_premises.premise: Being wedded to one macro model produces false alarms (post-GFC QE did not cause rampant inflation) and doomsday forecasts are often wrong (Covid fell sharply but recovered faster than expected); prices should be the null hypothesis, and one should not chase data releases such as PCE because the price reaction to them is what drives positions.
worldview_premises.support: Book 'Stocks, Crisis and False Alarms' (as relayed), QE and Covid examples.

worldview_premises.premise: Large language models add little to time-series forecasting, and machine learning does well in expansions but poorly in recessions because training data have few recessions, so model building is harder than expected.
worldview_premises.support: Two papers he cites from his blog; no details given.

worldview_premises.premise: Prices are public and discounted almost immediately, so models and new techniques are valuable only if they turn the same public data into private insight others do not have; new techniques should be adopted gradually, not as an on/off switch.
worldview_premises.support: Information-theory and efficient-markets reasoning.

worldview_premises.premise: The law of small numbers (gambler's fallacy and hot hand) affects trend and quant models that decide on limited data; knowing the distribution implies mean reversion, not knowing it implies following the hot hand.
worldview_premises.support: Behavioural finance literature (basketball and coin examples).

decision_process.practice: Add markets carefully, favouring two-sided markets with hedgers, some retail participation, established history and sufficient volume/open interest; avoid brand-new markets and markets with heavy central-bank intervention (lower exposure).
decision_process.why: Removing markets later is hard to decide well; one-sided or purely professional markets are harder to profit in.

decision_process.practice: Drop a market when volume or open interest falls below a threshold (jump risk), but not because it lost money for years; when reviewing, check how it earned or lost (one trade or many, choppiness).
decision_process.why: A losing market may be a diversifier; the future is unknown; cocoa shows explosive returns can follow years of losses.

decision_process.practice: Use backtests to probe the manager's assumptions, cost treatment and realism, and move from lab to factory (inputs, outputs, timing, costs, execution), not to judge by Sharpe.
decision_process.why: Every backtest looks good; carefulness is what is informative.

decision_process.practice: Prefer simple rules over regression or model-based signals.
Build the portfolio for diversification across many markets and treat it as the one free lunch.
decision_process.why: Applying a model across many markets and combining them is where the system value lies.

decision_process.practice: Build risk management into entry and exit rules and keep a stop loss as a fail-safe protecting investor principal.
decision_process.why: Plans fail when you are 'punched in the nose'.

decision_process.practice: Where stock and bond valuation or macro arguments conflict, follow price trends; use prices as the null hypothesis and depart only if needed.
decision_process.why: Macro models give false alarms; the price reaction to data matters, not the data.

decision_process.practice: Monitor stock-bond correlation (off-diagonal covariance terms) in a 60/40 portfolio.
decision_process.why: Positive correlation raises portfolio volatility and removes bond diversification.

decision_process.practice: Check sample size and distribution to avoid the law of small numbers in trend or quant models.
decision_process.why: Decisions are made on limited data; extrapolation and mean reversion are both mis-specified without the distribution.

decision_process.practice: Classify strategies by equity correlation, drawdown mitigation versus equities and alpha after beta.
decision_process.why: Tells loss mitigation from equity substitutes; trend following meets all three.

speakers.evidence_style: Practitioner anecdote and manager-evaluation experience, plus citation of papers (Hudson Bay, GIC/JPMorgan, LLM time-series and ML across the cycle papers, a book on macro false alarms); argues from first principles on information and diversification; offers few numbers himself.

current_views.view: US growth has been strong and disinflation slow because Treasury bill issuance offsets Fed tightening (a plausible explanation he wants to explore).
current_views.reasoning: Hudson Bay paper relayed; more near-money and fewer coupons.

current_views.view: US stocks look overvalued (mega-cap stocks well extended) while the Fed may cut as early as September, so there are compelling arguments for both stocks and bonds and prices should be followed.
current_views.reasoning: Cannot resolve the valuation question; trend following lets the market decide.

current_views.view: Trend following's recent three-month weakness does not mean much on its own ('three months don't make a year'); calm rate and inflation volatility is the cost of crisis alpha.
current_views.reasoning: Low rate and inflation volatility with sideways markets hurts trend; investors forget the crisis benefit.

current_views.view: The GIC/JPMorgan framework is one of the best explanations for holding trend following, even though the paper was agnostic.
current_views.reasoning: Trend meets all three criteria (low correlation, drawdown mitigation, alpha).

current_views.view: LLMs and machine learning deserve caution for systematic modelling.
current_views.reasoning: Two papers: no gain from LLMs in time series; ML poor in recessions.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers gave back performance for three months through July 2024, which strains investor conversations but opens entry points because too few investors hold trend following (and those who do hold too little).
worldview_premises.support: Industry observation; his optimist case.

worldview_premises.premise: If macro calms again (inflation and rates controlled by central banks), trend followers may struggle as in the decade to 2019.
worldview_premises.support: Historical analogy; he says he is not sure 'we're there yet'.

worldview_premises.premise: July 2024 was a transition period with reversals across currencies (yen strength), equities, metals, energy and bonds; the Trend Barometer at 36 signals a weak environment and a negative month for trend followers.

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility floors and multiple lookbacks are needed so that suppressed volatility (Swiss franc, short rates) does not lead to oversized positions; large managers look at volatility over several time frames.
worldview_premises.support: Practitioner knowledge of large managers.

worldview_premises.premise: Removing markets for past losses is dangerous: cocoa was unprofitable for trend followers for 15 to 20 years before January 2023 and then extremely profitable in 2023 to 2024; a market that makes little money but pays when others lose still adds diversification value.
worldview_premises.support: Cocoa episode.

worldview_premises.premise: A trend follower should add a market only if its diversification value exceeds its transaction costs and the opportunity cost of displacing other markets (listener Philip's framing, adopted as a trade-off).
worldview_premises.support: Read from a listener's email; the hosts discuss rather than endorse it as their own rule.

worldview_premises.support: Observed data; no figure given.

worldview_premises.premise: Every technology wave in 30 years was predicted to hurt trend following and it has not; experience is hard to backtest.
worldview_premises.support: Three decades of industry experience; hedged ('one should never say never').

disagreements.topic: Removing markets from a trend portfolio

positions.speaker: Mark rinsky (caption spelling; Systematic Investor co-host)
positions.position: Run regular reviews with explicit drop criteria (falling volume or open interest, loss of two-sidedness, choppiness) but never drop for past losses alone; invest the effort in adding markets carefully.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Liquidity is the clear reason to drop; volatility issues are better handled with volatility floors and multiple lookbacks than by removal; the bigger risk is removing markets for losses (cocoa).

disagreements.topic: Cocoa: poor trend market in principle, or underrated diversifier?

positions.speaker: Mark rinsky (caption spelling; Systematic Investor co-host)
positions.position: Government-managed pricing and choppiness give several reasons not to trade cocoa, yet a supply dislocation produced explosive returns, so exclusion would have hurt.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Cocoa was unprofitable for 15 to 20 years then extremely profitable; this is the example of why not to remove markets for losses; it made some managers' profits.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The Hudson Bay bill-issuance argument is relayed from a paper with no numbers, no estimate of the QE-equivalent size, and no test of the claim that it explains US growth and slow disinflation; Mark says he wants to explore it more.

Mark's conclusion that trend following meets all three GIC/JPM criteria rests on the paper's strategy-level 'managed futures' category; he himself notes managed futures is not the same as trend following, yet applies the result to trend following. The paper's authors did not draw this conclusion.

Mark uses 'prices as the null hypothesis' and 'follow prices' after saying that valuation and macro arguments for stocks and bonds are both compelling; the claim that trend following resolves the conflict is argued, not shown, and ignores the cost of whipsaws he himself describes in calm regimes.

The market-review criteria (retail share, two-sidedness) are unquantified and some conflict with the 'don't drop for losses' rule; the cocoa case is both a reason to exclude (managed prices) and a poster child for inclusion.
Claims about papers on LLMs in time series and ML in recessions are second-hand and the first paper's test is described as 'very specific'; the extrapolation to a general caution is Mark's.

The host says he is not sure trend followers are in a calm-macro regime yet, while also saying inflation concerns have eased and rates are subdued; the PCE number released during recording was higher than expected, which neither speaker connects to the thesis.
Stock-bond correlation risk is raised by both speakers but no threshold or response rule is given beyond 'follow trends' or 'think about valuation'.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs the speakers treat as relevant: the mix of Treasury bill and coupon issuance versus Fed QT runoff (net duration supply) for financial conditions; rate and inflation volatility (calm hurts trend); the one-year rolling stock-bond correlation (portfolio risk and the case for trend); volume and open interest by market (jump risk); and the price reaction to data rather than data themselves. Horizon is not stated precisely: a few months for trend giveback and entry points, and a multi-year regime view for calm versus volatile macro. Neither speaker makes a price forecast.
reader_inferences: (reader) Mark's view of trend following is mainly structural: it earns its place through diversification and crisis behaviour, so the cost is regime-dependent (calm periods) and the right response to drawdowns is to look at the process, not the recent returns.

(reader) The cocoa case plays two roles: for Mark it shows exclusion risk despite good reasons to dislike the market; for Niels it shows removal for past losses is dangerous. Both lead to 'keep broad coverage, drop for liquidity'.

(reader) The T-bill argument implies that Fed policy alone understates financial-condition easing; a trend follower reading rates would see the effect in curve moves, not in the policy rate, consistent with 'let prices speak'.
(reader) The backtest-as-diligence argument shifts the investor's question from 'how good are the numbers' to 'how were they produced', which links to the law-of-small-numbers advice on sample size.
